draft_ledger.reference_answer:
Across the available PFAS analytical workflows, several distinct blank types and their roles in contamination assessment are described, but the information is limited to a small number of studies and does not support generalizing a single standard frequency of blank use.

For blank types and uses (T01):

• In a full-scale AO-MBR-RO municipal WWTP PFAS study, multiple blanks were implemented to monitor contamination associated with both sampling and analysis. Specifically, “Field blanks, transport blanks, and procedural blanks were prepared for each batch of samples to monitor potential contamination during sampling and analysis.” This links field blanks and transport blanks to assessing contamination introduced during sample collection and transport, and procedural blanks to contamination that could arise from the overall sample preparation procedure. In the same workflow, solvent blanks were used to address the analytical system itself: “Solvent blanks (methanol and acetonitrile) were also analyzed to ensure instrumental cleanliness.” Here, the solvent blanks serve to detect or rule out PFAS-related background originating from the solvents and instrument pathway, thereby assessing instrumental cleanliness.

• In a PFAS sorption study relevant to AFFF-impacted groundwater, the analytical sequence incorporated additional blank types that function as sequence-level quality controls for contamination and instrument behavior. The authors report: “Double blanks (without surrogate nor standards), blanks (with surrogate but not standards), and quality control (QC) samples (with surrogates and standards) were included in the analytical sequence every 8 −10 samples to ensure minimal contamination and adequate MS performance.” Double blanks (no surrogate, no standards) and blanks (with surrogate, no standards) therefore act as checks for contamination and mass spectrometer performance within the sequence. Their background signals directly inform data acceptance: “Only signals (i.e., peak areas) greater than 10 times any background signals observed in the blanks or double blanks were considered acceptable and used for subsequent data analysis.” This shows that these blanks are explicitly used to quantify background and to set a threshold for acceptable signal, linking them tightly to contamination and background assessment.

These excerpts collectively document use of field blanks, transport blanks, procedural blanks, solvent blanks, and analytical-sequence blanks (double blanks and blanks with surrogates) in PFAS workflows. They demonstrate how each is applied to assess different contamination pathways: sampling and transport, laboratory handling, solvent/instrument background, and ongoing sequence background and mass spectrometer performance.

For blank frequency and reporting consistency (T02):

• In the WWTP PFAS study, the reported frequency is at the batch level: “Field blanks, transport blanks, and procedural blanks were prepared for each batch of samples to monitor potential contamination during sampling and analysis.” This indicates that every analytical batch included these blanks, but the excerpt does not state a universal number of blanks per batch beyond this per-batch preparation statement. Solvent blanks were also analyzed, although their exact numerical frequency is not detailed beyond their inclusion for instrumental cleanliness.

• In the PFAS sorption study, blank inclusion is reported on an analytical-sequence basis: “Double blanks (without surrogate nor standards), blanks (with surrogate but not standards), and quality control (QC) samples (with surrogates and standards) were included in the analytical sequence every 8 −10 samples to ensure minimal contamination and adequate MS performance.” This specifies that double blanks and blanks recur every 8–10 samples. Furthermore, these blanks are operationally integrated into data quality criteria, as “Only signals (i.e., peak areas) greater than 10 times any background signals observed in the blanks or double blanks were considered acceptable and used for subsequent data analysis.”

Comparing these two studies shows that blank frequency and implementation are described in study-specific terms: one workflow uses per-batch field, transport, and procedural blanks plus solvent blanks, while another uses double blanks and blanks every 8–10 samples in the analytical sequence. The available evidence thus supports that PFAS analysts may employ multiple blank types for contamination assessment and instrument cleanliness, but it does not justify inferring a single, universal frequency (e.g., a standard number of procedural blanks per batch) or a uniform reporting practice across the broader PFAS literature. Any broader assessment of consistency or variability in blank frequency reporting would require additional studies beyond those cited here.

draft_ledger.reference_answer:
PFAS and related PFC analytical methods do describe background contamination risks associated with LC hardware, but they do so at a general level rather than by pinpointing specific PTFE parts.

One wastewater PFAS study reports that "instrument parts were also replaced with materials such as stainless steel or polyetheretherketone (PEEK) to prevent any back-ground contamination" [NQ09_MMG001]. This shows that the authors regarded instrument hardware as a potential source of background PFAS contamination and chose stainless steel or PEEK components as cleaner alternatives, without identifying any particular part as always being responsible. Another PFAS-related LC–MS method notes that "several precautions were taken to minimize PFC contamination in the system such as the use of stainless steel or PEEK lines" [NQ09_MMG002], again indicating concern about contamination from the LC lines themselves and the use of PEEK or stainless steel to mitigate it. Together, these methods support a general view that PFAS/PFC contamination can arise from LC instrument parts or lines and that switching to stainless steel or PEEK components is a common precaution, but they do not single out specific components as universal contamination sources.

Regarding explicit evidence for replacing particular PTFE components with PEEK, the available texts are more limited. The wastewater PFAS study describes replacing generic "instrument parts" with stainless steel or PEEK [NQ09_MMG001], and the advanced oxidation study mentions stainless steel or PEEK "lines" [NQ09_MMG002], but neither document states that the original parts or lines were PTFE, nor do they name specific elements such as particular valves, fittings, or solvent lines. Thus, they support the idea that replacing unspecified LC components with PEEK can be part of a contamination-control strategy, but they do not provide component-level, PTFE-specific replacement evidence.

System-level verification of contamination control is documented in the wastewater study. After implementing measures including replacement of instrument parts with stainless steel or PEEK, the authors prepared "field blanks, transport blanks, and procedural blanks" and also ran "solvent blanks" [NQ09_MMG001]. They report that "across all blank samples, PFAS concentrations were below the method's limit of quantification (LOQ), confirming negligible contamination" [NQ09_MMG001]. This demonstrates tracing and verification at the level of the whole analytical workflow: the combined precautions, including the material changes, produced negligible measurable PFAS contamination in blanks. However, this approach does not isolate which specific component(s) originally contributed contamination, nor does it establish that a single, fixed set of component replacements—much less any particular PTFE-to-PEEK swap—will resolve PFAS contamination in all LC systems.

Overall, the cited PFAS analytical studies support general concern about hardware-derived PFAS/PFC contamination and the use of stainless steel or PEEK parts and lines to reduce it, with system-level blank checks to verify low contamination. They do not, however, provide explicit, PTFE-identified, component-level replacement evidence or a universally applicable component-replacement recipe.

In the PFAS methods illustrated, isotope‑labelled internal standards are incorporated directly into the sample‑preparation and LC‑MS/MS workflow to support isotope‑dilution quantification and control analytical bias.

For target PFAS analysis, isotope‑labelled internal standards are added early in the workflow so they experience the same extraction and concentration steps as the native analytes. In one protocol, “Isotope-labelled internal standards will be added at the start of sample preparation, typically at 10 ng ⋅ L⁻¹, to enable isotope-dilution quantification” [NQ11_MMG001]. In another study, LC‑MS/MS analysis of groundwater used “an isotope dilution technique … for the PFAS compounds of interest using carbon-13 and/or oxygen-18 labeled analogs to allow for the correction of analytical bias encountered with chemically complex environmental samples” [NQ11_MMG002]. These examples show that isotope‑labelled standards are introduced before analysis and used in isotope‑dilution calculations to obtain quantitative results while correcting for matrix‑related analytical bias, thereby improving data quality.

The choice between exact and non‑exact isotope‑labelled standards is linked to which PFAS are targeted and how broad the method’s scope is. Where an identically labelled analog exists, it can be used directly. However, the groundwater study explicitly notes that “Compounds that do not have an identically labeled analog were quantitated using a closely related labeled analog” [NQ11_MMG002]. This indicates that, to maintain coverage when the target list includes PFAS lacking exact labelled standards, the method substitutes structurally similar labeled analogs. In broader AFFF studies that include both target and suspect PFAS, the internal standards for suspect compounds are chosen from an existing target list rather than being exact analogs. For semiquantitative suspect analysis, “concentrations were estimated with a target calibrant and an internal standard from the target analyte list, selected based upon the ionizable functional group and fluoroalkyl chain length” [NQ11_MMG003]. Similarly, another AFFF study assigned “quantifiable PFAAs … to be the internal standards of unsaturated perfluoroalkyl acids (U‑PFAAs) and keto perfluoroalkyl acids (K‑PFAAs), and the internal standards of specific compounds within these classes were matched based on their fluorocarbon chain length (e.g., PFBA to U‑PFBA and K‑PFBA, and PFOA to U‑PFOA and K‑PFOA)” [NQ11_MMG004]. These approaches tie internal‑standard choice to PFAS class and chain length so that a finite set of labeled or quantifiable PFAAs can support measurement of a broader range of PFAS, aligning internal‑standard selection with the method’s analyte coverage.

Non‑exact isotope‑labelled or class‑representative analogs are therefore relied upon in several specific situations. In the ion‑exchange/electrochemical oxidation groundwater study, whenever a PFAS “do[es] not have an identically labeled analog” it “was quantitated using a closely related labeled analog” [NQ11_MMG002], showing that structurally related labeled standards are used to obtain quantitative results for PFAS beyond those with exact labels. In suspect‑screening workflows for AFFF, where many PFAS do not have individual calibrated standards, “semiquantitative analysis of suspect analytes” is performed by estimating concentrations “with a target calibrant and an internal standard from the target analyte list, selected based upon the ionizable functional group and fluoroalkyl chain length” [NQ11_MMG003]. Likewise, in class‑based analysis of novel PFAS such as U‑PFAAs and K‑PFAAs, “quantifiable PFAAs were assigned to be the internal standards” for those classes, with assignments matched by “fluorocarbon chain length,” and after assigning an internal‑standard peak area to each suspect PFAS, “the suspect’s concentration was calculated based on the target PFAS’s calibration curve” [NQ11_MMG004]. These examples illustrate that, when expanding beyond a narrow set of targets or when exact labeled analogs are unavailable, studies rely on non‑exact, structurally or class‑matched internal standards for quantitative or semiquantitative PFAS analysis.

Across these studies, the internal‑standard and labeled‑standard sets are defined for specific PFAS compound lists (e.g., “PFAS compounds of interest” [NQ11_MMG002] or a particular “target analyte list” [NQ11_MMG003]) and specific PFAS classes such as U‑PFAAs and K‑PFAAs [NQ11_MMG004]. The evidence does not indicate that any one exact isotope‑labelled standard set would be sufficient for all PFAS analytical methods; rather, internal‑standard selection is tailored to the targeted PFAS and the scope of each method.

draft_ledger.reference_answer:
Across the reported studies, PFAS recovery from complex water and wastewater matrices is quantitatively documented and clearly matrix- and analyte-dependent, and final concentration reporting employs validated approaches to correct for recovery and matrix effects.

For municipal wastewater effluent spiked with PFAS, Zheng et al. report high, near-quantitative recoveries for three individual PFAS. In PFAS-spiked municipal wastewater effluent, recovery percentages were 100±3% and 97±4% for PFOA, 91±10% and 96±10% for PFOS, and 95±9% and 94±6% for PFBA, and this was interpreted as indicating limited influence of the municipal wastewater effluent matrix relative to DDI water (NQ13_MMG001: “the corresponding recovery percentages were 100± 3% and 97± 4% for PFOA, 91± 10% and 96± 10% for PFOS, and 95± 9% and 94± 6% for PFBA… This result potentially indicated the limited influence of municipal wastewater effluent matrices compared to DDI water.”). These values show that, in this particular effluent and for these specific PFAS, recoveries are close to 100% but still differ somewhat by analyte.

In contrast, Habib et al. demonstrate that recovery is substantially lower and more affected by matrix in other wastewater matrices for PFCAs using a stir bar sorptive extraction method. For wastewater influent, recovery rates were significantly lower, with values from 29% (±12) to 44% (±11) at the 10 ng spike level and between 21% (±7) and 31% (±10) at the 20 ng level, indicating a substantial matrix effect due to interfering substances (NQ13_MMG003: “recovery rates in wastewater influent were significantly lower, with values from 29% (±12) to 44% (±11) at the 10 ng level, and … between 21% (±7) and 31% (±10). This indicates a substantial matrix effect”). For wastewater effluent in the same study, recoveries were intermediate: 10 ng spikes yielded 43% (±6) to 65% (±14), and 20 ng spikes gave 44% (±11) to 74% (±8) (NQ13_MMG003: “Wastewater effluent displayed intermediate recovery rates. The 10 ng spikes yielded 43% (±6) to 65% (±14) recoveries and the 20 ng spikes led to 44% ( ±11) to 74% (±8) recoveries.”). These results confirm that the extraction efficiency of PFCAs is strongly impacted by matrix complexity and that recovery varies both with matrix type (influent vs effluent) and analyte/spike level.

Taken together, these studies illustrate that PFAS and PFCA recovery cannot be represented by a single universal value across complex water matrices: some municipal wastewater effluents support recoveries near 100% for particular PFAS, whereas more complex matrices such as wastewater influent yield recoveries as low as roughly 20–40%, with effluents giving intermediate values. Recovery performance is therefore both matrix- and analyte-dependent.

Regarding how recovery and matrix effects are handled in final PFAS concentration calculations, different validated analytical strategies are employed. In a field demonstration of PFAS treatment in groundwater, Liang et al. corrected for analytical bias and matrix effects using isotope dilution. Water samples were extracted using SPE and analyzed by LC-MS/MS, and “an isotope dilution technique was employed for the PFAS compounds of interest using carbon-13 and/or oxygen-18 labeled analogs to allow for the correction of analytical bias encountered with chemically complex environmental samples,” while “compounds that do not have an identically labeled analog were quantitated using a closely related labeled analog” (NQ13_MMG002). In this approach, the labeled internal standards co-extracted and co-eluted with each target PFAS provide compound-specific or closely related surrogates that account for recovery and matrix suppression or enhancement, so that the reported PFAS concentrations are corrected for analytical bias in the complex groundwater matrix.

In the PFCA wastewater work, Habib et al. explicitly link the observed low recovery and strong matrix effects in influent and intermediate recoveries in effluent to the need for matrix-aware quantification strategies. To address matrix effects in more complex wastewater samples, they propose using standard addition: “the standard addition method could be considered a viable solution. By adding known quantities of PFCAs directly to the samples, this method compensates for matrix-induced deviations. This allows for a more accurate quantification of analytes” (NQ13_MMG003). Here, calibration is performed in the sample itself, so the measured response inherently incorporates the matrix-induced recovery and signal modification, yielding final concentrations that are effectively corrected for those matrix-specific biases.

Across these examples, recovery is explicitly measured and reported for specific PFAS and PFCAs in defined complex matrices, and variability by matrix and analyte is clearly documented. Final concentration reporting makes use of validated correction logic—either via isotope dilution with appropriately chosen labeled analogs or via standard addition—to compensate for recovery losses and matrix-induced analytical bias. The data do not support assuming any single expected recovery percentage as valid for all PFAS across all complex water or wastewater matrices; instead, recovery and correction strategies are tailored to the particular matrix and target analytes.
